title: 3-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping for Grade 3 (Borrowing Across Zeros Made Easy) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn 3 digit subtraction with regrouping for Grade 3, including borrowing across zeros like 700 - 258, with a free 8-question quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Column subtraction stalls the moment a child meets 452 − 187 or a row of zeros like 700 − 258. Here is the written method that fixes it, why exchanging works, and how to check every answer — plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A Grade 3 student writes 452 − 187 in neat columns, reaches the ones place and stares: 2 take away 7. ‘You can’t do it,’ she says, then writes 5 anyway — 7 minus 2, the wrong way round. That single slip, flipping the digits because the top one looks too small, is the most common error children make in 3 digit subtraction with regrouping grade 3 teachers see every single year. The fix is not more speed drills. It is understanding what borrowing actually does to the number.

By Grade 3 children step up from two-digit sums to full column subtraction of 3- and 4-digit numbers, and regrouping (older textbooks call it borrowing) is the skill that decides whether they get there. I have taught this to a lot of eight-year-olds, and the ones who struggle almost never have a calculation problem. They have a place-value problem. Get the place value clear and the exchanging looks after itself.

What ‘regrouping’ actually means

A number like 452 is not ‘four hundred, five, two’. It is 4 hundreds, 5 tens and 2 ones. Regrouping is nothing more than trading one unit for ten of the next size down: one ten becomes ten ones, one hundred becomes ten tens. When the top digit in a column is smaller than the bottom digit you cannot subtract yet, so you go next door and exchange. Ten ones arrive in the ones column, the tens column drops by one, and suddenly the subtraction works.

I insist on the word ‘exchange’ in class. ‘Borrow’ hints that you hand it back later, which you never do — you have simply written the same number a different way. Most NCERT-aligned textbooks now say regrouping for exactly this reason, and it is worth using the same word at home.

A worked example of 3 digit subtraction with regrouping

Take 452 − 187. Set it up in columns, ones under ones, and always work right to left — never left to right, because a later column can change an earlier one.

ColumnWhat you faceThe exchangeDigit written
Ones2 − 7 (too small)Take 1 ten from the 5 tens; ones become 1212 − 7 = 5
Tens4 − 8 (too small)Take 1 hundred from the 4 hundreds; tens become 1414 − 8 = 6
Hundreds3 − 1No exchange needed3 − 1 = 2

The answer is 265. Notice the 5 tens dropped to 4, then the 4 hundreds dropped to 3 — each exchange leaves a smaller digit behind. If a child forgets to cross out and reduce that neighbour, the whole answer goes wrong from that point on.

The hard case: subtracting across a zero

700 − 258 is where a lot of children freeze, and fair enough — there is nothing next door to borrow from. Ones: 0 − 8, no. Tens: also 0, so you cannot take a ten from there either. You have to travel two columns to reach the 7 hundreds.

Do it as a chain. Take one hundred from the 7, leaving 6 hundreds; that hundred becomes 10 tens. Now take one of those tens, leaving 9 tens; that ten becomes 10 ones. The 700 has been rewritten as 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones — the same value, just regrouped. Now every column subtracts cleanly: 10 − 8 = 2, 9 − 5 = 4, 6 − 2 = 4. Answer: 442.

The quick way to think about zeros

Once children have done a few, teach the shortcut: when you cross a zero, it turns into 9 and passes the exchange along. The single hundred you borrowed feeds both the tens and the ones. Four-digit numbers work the same way — 1000 − 476 rewrites 1000 as 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones, giving 524.

Always check by adding back

Subtraction and addition undo each other, and this is the most useful habit you can build. If 700 − 258 = 442, then 442 + 258 must return 700. Add the answer to the number you took away; if you land back on the number you started with, you were right. It takes ten seconds and catches almost every regrouping slip. I make it a rule: no subtraction is finished until it has been added back.

Common mistakes I see every year

  • Flipping the column: writing 7 − 2 because 2 − 7 ‘can’t be done’, instead of exchanging.
  • Forgetting to reduce the neighbour after borrowing, so the tens or hundreds stays too big.
  • Trying to borrow from a zero as if it had something to give, rather than travelling on to the next non-zero digit.
  • Lining up digits carelessly so ones sit under tens — graph paper or a squared notebook fixes this instantly.
  • Skipping the add-back check and never noticing the answer is off by exactly ten or a hundred.

Below is a free, eight-question quiz covering exactly what we worked through — column subtraction with exchanging, the tricky zeros, and checking by adding back. faq.q: What is the difference between borrowing and regrouping?
faq.a: They describe the same step. ‘Borrowing’ is the older word; ‘regrouping’ or ‘exchanging’ is the NCERT-aligned term used today. You trade one unit for ten of the next place value — one ten for ten ones, or one hundred for ten tens.

faq.q: How do you subtract across a zero, like 700 − 258?
faq.a: You cannot borrow from a zero, so travel to the next non-zero digit. In 700, take one hundred from the 7 (leaving 6), turn it into 10 tens, then move one ten to the ones. 700 becomes 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones, and every column subtracts cleanly.

faq.q: Why does my child keep getting the wrong answer even with regrouping?
faq.a: The usual cause is forgetting to reduce the neighbouring column after borrowing, or flipping a column (writing 7 − 2 instead of exchanging for 12 − 7). Squared paper for straight columns and an add-back check catch almost all of these.

faq.q: How can a Grade 3 child check a subtraction answer?
faq.a: Add the answer back to the number that was taken away. If 700 − 258 = 442, then 442 + 258 should equal 700. Landing back on the starting number confirms the answer is right.
